newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia cattle kill hit by live export boom.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia cattle kill hit by live export boom.

text.p: Burgeoning live cattle exports have contributed to a decline in Australia's cattle slaughter levels this year, the Australian Meat and Livestock Corp (AMLC) said in its October Meat and Livestock Review released on Wednesday.

Slaughterings for the January/August were 3.5 percent below those of the previous corresponding period, with Queensland on a 12 percent decline, the AMLC said in a review of the cattle and beef market. Queensland processors were being affected by the drain on cattle supplies for the live cattle trade, AMLC said.

For the year to September, Queensland's live cattle exports had increased by 53 percent to 554,352 head, AMLC said. "These figures translate into a large number of bullocks that will not be available for slaughter in coming years," it said.
Kill rates throughout Queensland in September and early October were 18 percent down on last year's level, it said.

AMLC's latest comments show that Australia's live cattle exports continue to boom. Australia's total live cattle exports for 1997/97 to June 30 are expected to exceed 750,000 head, an increase of 500 percent or 520,000 since 1988.
Presentations to the recent New South Wales Farmers' Association annual conference showed that Australia's live cattle exports have been growing strongly in response to high domestic slaughter costs.
The AMLC said in its latest review that good rainfall during the past month had given Queensland the best start to a wet season for the cattle industry in many years.
Average to above-average rainfall predictions for a large area of southern and northern Australia suggested it could be the best season in many years, the AMLC said.
The wet season, apart from restricting supplies in many areas, had lifted prospects of a general improvement in pasture conditions and encouraged some restocking, it said.
A 12.3 percent increase in cow prices across Queensland during September was evidence of increased restocker activity, it said.
In the same month, the price of Australian steers to Japan rose by 6.5 percent while the price of steers to Korea rose 5.6 percent.
The AMLC said a mild but sustained recovery in Japan over the last six weeks had lifted prices in the Japanese wholesale market for chilled Australian grassfed fullsets by 43 percent.

The price rises were the result of an acute shortage of chilled product and of attempts by Japanese trading houses to recoup some financial losses on beef stocks -- rather than a reflection in a surge in consumer demand, the AMLC said.

Beef shipments from Australia to Japan in September totalled only 15,962 tonnes, the lowest monthly total since February 1992, it said. This provided evidence of difficulties facing Australian exporters to Japan in September, it said.
The frozen beef market in Japan continued to be hampered by large beef inventories, but there were weak signs that the markety was beginning to lift, the corporation said.
Consumer demand in Japan should continue to improve as beef consumption rose toward the end of the year, it said.
